questions.stem: The poem is mostly written in the future tense ('One day soon he'll tell her…'). What is the effect?

options.A: It shows the poem is set a hundred years from now.
options.B: It suggests the move is certain to happen because it has happened so many times before.
options.C: It shows the family is planning a holiday.
options.D: It suggests the move will never happen.

questions.explanation: Describing what 'will' happen, step by step, shows the speaker knows exactly how it goes: the family has moved many times before.

distractors.C: they are packing up to move, not holidaying
distractors.D: the details show it is certain

questions.stem: Why are the children 'wildly excited' about the move?

options.A: They have been told they will go to a better school.
options.B: They are going to live near the beach.
options.C: Their father has bought them a new puppy.
options.D: For the children, moving feels like an adventure.

questions.explanation: The poem says they get excited 'for no reason': to children, packing up seems thrilling, unlike for their mother.

distractors.B: the poem doesn't say where they are going
distractors.C: the kelpie pup is already theirs

questions.stem: What does the mother picking all the green tomatoes suggest?

options.A: She is making tomato sauce for a party.
options.B: She prefers green tomatoes to red ones.
options.C: The move is happening before her garden is ready, and she won't leave anything behind.

questions.explanation: Green tomatoes are not ripe. She has to pick them early because they are leaving before her garden can be enjoyed: a sign of her disappointment.

questions.stem: The oldest girl is close to tears 'because she was happy here', and the youngest is beaming 'because she wasn't'. What does this contrast show?

options.B: The youngest girl is always cheerful.
options.C: The family is moving to be closer to friends.
options.D: Each move affects family members differently.

questions.explanation: The same event brings sadness to one daughter and joy to the other: the poem shows how differently people feel about leaving.

distractors.B: she's happy because she wasn't happy there
distractors.C: no reason for the move is given

questions.stem: Many lines begin with 'And'. What is the effect of this?

options.A: It makes the events pile up one after another, like a familiar routine.
options.B: It makes the poem sound like a song for children.
options.D: It shows the speaker is confused.

questions.explanation: Repeating 'And' links each event to the next, building a list that feels like a well-known, repeated pattern.

distractors.C: starting lines with 'And' doesn't create rhyme
distractors.D: the speaker is clear and calm
distractors.B: the tone is sad and grown-up

questions.stem: What does the title 'Drifters' suggest about the family?

options.A: They move from place to place without settling anywhere for long.
options.B: They are lost in the bush.
options.C: They like to sleep in late.

questions.explanation: A drifter moves around without a fixed home, like something drifting on water. Dawe said the poem drew on his mother's longing for a settled home.

distractors.B: they choose to move; they aren't lost

passages.title: Drifters – Bruce Dawe
passages.intro: Find and read this poem before you start.
passages.credit: The poem is still in copyright, so it is not printed here.
paragraphs: Read 'Drifters' by Bruce Dawe. It is in Bruce Dawe's collection 'Sometimes Gladness' and in many school anthologies; you can also find it by searching the title and poet online.
The poem imagines a family about to move house yet again.
Keep the poem open next to this app while you answer. Read it twice: once for the story, once for how it is written.
